en: The Illustrated Chart of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma and the Determination of the Patriarchs, Scroll One, including the Preface, composed by the Song Dynasty śramaṇa Chén Sēngqìsōng of Tánjīn Dōngshān.
Preface: To begin with, Bodhidharma was truly the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Buddha’s single teaching.
Together with Mahākāśyapa,
he is one who directly inherited the transmission from Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
It was transmitted to China;
as many years and generations have passed,
the genealogical records have become erroneous and confused.
Yet scholars of little discernment are unable to infer and examine its fundamental source; thus,
they truly fail to understand it.
Conflicting and divergent opinions have prevailed throughout both ancient and modern times;
throughout his life, Qisong regarded this as his greatest affliction.
Having duly examined right and wrong and rectified the ancestral lineage,
his writings were about to be issued;
it coincided with the distribution of the charts of the Patriarchs’ transmission of the Dharma and the conferral of the robe.
This was promulgated throughout the empire;
yet although all who study Buddhism honored it,
they remained bewildered and failed to comprehend the Emperor’s intent.
Qisong is fortunate in this regard;
he privately says to those who understand:
"Our Buddha took the essentials of the True Dharma as the primary tenet of the Great Teaching."
Taking the secret transmission as the progenitor of this great teaching,
its school is the source of the Way of the sages and worthies,
and the wondrous foundation of all living beings in heaven and earth.
His patriarch is the great paradigm for those who study and practice śīla, samādhi, and prajñā for ten thousand generations;
he is the true verification of the teachings of the twelve divisions of the canon.
Since the transmission of the scriptures became disordered, they have remained obscure and blurred.
The world has harbored doubts regarding this for nearly a thousand years.
Now, His Majesty, the Great Sage,
has specially issued this diagram to rectify the lineage of its ancestral progenitor.
However, as for the teachings of the Sages,
it is only the Sages themselves who can rectify them.
Is this not indeed the great fortune of the followers of the Buddha for ten thousand generations?
This is also a great fortune for Heaven, Earth, and all living beings.
Thus, Qisong, disregarding the risk of being punished for his audacity and foolishness,
ventures, despite his ignorance, to cite these ancient precedents.
I have extrapolated the intent of the supreme sages and respectfully annotated the Patriarchal Chart;
this is precisely what was previously distributed concerning the transmission of the Dharma and the conferral of the robe by the Patriarchs.
However, as for that which first brought disorder to our ancestral school and deluded the scholars of the world,
none is more so than the *Dharma-paryāya-dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (The Record of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury).
To rectify the fundamental lineage and resolve the disputes of ten thousand generations,
nothing is more suitable than the *Canyijing* (Sūtra on Dhyāna). Indeed,
the *Canyijing* predates the *Fofa chuan* (Tradition of the Dharma Transmission).
The sixty-two years [of the transmission] are complete from beginning to end;
as for the twenty-eight patriarchs,
they have already appeared during the Jin dynasty.
The *Fufa zhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma Transmission) dates from after the Emperor Zhenjun abolished the teachings;
it is incomplete, noting only twenty-four generations until the time of the Wei dynasty.
It was precisely because of his meditative experience that the *Dharma-paryāya-vaṃśa* (The Transmission of the Dharma-treasury) is indeed erroneous.
If it were the case that the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma exclusively to Mahākāśyapa...
I have then presented the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
and the *Dhyāna Sūtras*, along with their prefaces;
one may seek the truth therein by means of one's own insight.
Yet the subtle purport of the Buddha remains therein.
Your Majesty’s sagely nature is lofty and sublime;
you alone have attained that which lies beyond words and speech.
This was indeed his innate endowment and the Buddha’s prophecy;
therefore, when he expounded upon the patriarchs of Chan,
it was consistently in accord with the sutras.
It is fitting that this be transmitted for ten thousand generations,
serving forever as a definitive judgment for the Three Studies.
May the sons of the Buddha follow it and look up to it with reverence.
The world will no longer harbor doubts.
As for those depicted in the diagram,
they begin with Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa.
Reaching down to the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, Chan Master Dajian,
there are thirty-four positions in total;
furthermore, these include virtuous figures from both Confucianism and Buddhism who spoke of our ancestral masters.
There are ten individuals for whom there is existing evidence;
they are listed to the left of the various patriarchs,
following their entries in the *Zhengfajingzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma).
I have come to the palace gate to present this;
having troubled Your Majesty’s august favor,
I cannot bear the extreme of my trepidation and fear.
Respectfully preface:
The Primordial Patriarch Śākyamuni Buddha was manifested in birth in the kingdom of Central India.
As the son of the noble King Śuddhodana,
he immediately renounced the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
left the household life, realized the unsurpassed path, and turned the great wheel of Dharma.
Thereafter, when seventy-nine years had passed and he was on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted his Great Dharma Seal to his foremost disciple Mahākāśyapa,
and further commanded Ānanda to serve as his deputy in propagating the teachings.
Furthermore, he entrusted the golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe to Mahākāśyapa to pass on to the future Maitreya Buddha, who is to succeed him as the successor.
He spoke this verse:
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma; Without Dharma, even Dharma is Dharma.
Now, at the time of entrusting this absence of Dharma, How has any dharma ever been a dharma?
The First Patriarch Mahākāśyapa. The First Patriarch Mahākāśyapa.
He was originally a native of Magadha,
born of the Brahmin caste,
and his body was golden in color.
First, he left his home to enter the mountains and cultivated himself through the dhūta practices; subsequently,
he encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
He then returned to him and served as his disciple.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
he commanded the assembly of arhats to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.
Thereafter, he took up the Buddha’s robe and entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
he then transmitted the Dharma-seal to Ānanda.
A verse was spoken:
All phenomena are from the very beginning phenomena; There is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon.
How could there be phenomenon or non-phenomenon Within a single phenomenon?
The Second Patriarch, Ānanda,
was of the Kṣatriya caste and was the son of King Droṇodana.
He was the younger cousin of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Admiring the Buddha, he left the household life to become the Buddha’s attendant;
he was foremost among those who possess total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
He transmitted the Dharma taught by the Buddha;
like water being passed from one vessel to another,
he never once forgot or neglected it.
When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to his disciple Śāṇakavāsin and further charged Maudgalyāyana with its preservation.
A verse says:
The Dharma originally entrusted exists; Once entrusted, it is said that there is no dharma.
Each must awaken for themselves; Upon awakening, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
The Third Patriarch, Śāṇakavāsin (also known as Śanabasa),
was a native of Mathurā.
He was of the Viśākha clan; he remained in his mother’s womb for six years before being born.
He possessed natural garments that grew along with his body.
He left the household life to become a disciple of Ānanda.
Having received his prediction from the Buddha, he resided at the Uruvilvā Monastery;
first, he subdued the two fire-dragons of that land,
and thereafter he led the assembly to dwell there.
When he was about to enter nirvana,
he entrusted the Dharma to his disciple Upagupta,
speaking this verse:
Neither non-dharma nor mind; Neither mind nor dharma.
When speaking of these as "mind-dharmas," These dharmas are not mind-dharmas.
The Fourth Patriarch Upagupta. The Fourth Patriarch Upagupta.
He was a native of the country of Cālikā,
of the Śūdra clan,
and a disciple of Śāṇakavāsin.
Having left the household life, he attained the Way.
There were extraordinary signs,
and he was called the Buddha Without Physical Marks (Animitta-buddha).
He delivered the greatest number of people;
the tally of those he recorded filled the stone chamber.
He was about to enter nirvana.
He then entrusted the Dharma to his disciple, Diṭṭhaka, and spoke this verse:
"The mind is itself the primordial mind; the primordial mind is not a dharma that exists."
There is the Dharma, there is the fundamental mind; it is neither mind nor the fundamental Dharma.
The Fifth Patriarch, Diṭṭhagga (Tiḍuōjiā), was a native of Magadha; his surname remains unknown.
He first left the household life under the Venerable Guptaka.
While traveling to propagate the Dharma in Central India,
he encountered the Great Sage Mīḍhika, who recounted his own past karmic connections.
He sought to become his disciple.
When [the Buddha] was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he then entrusted the Dharma to Mijie (Mecaka).
A verse says:
To penetrate the dharma of the fundamental mind, There is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Awakening is the same as non-awakening; Without mind, there is also no dharma.
The Sixth Patriarch, Micchaka.
He was a native of Central India;
his clan name remains unknown.
At first, he grew weary of the arts of the immortals and sought out the master Tīṣya to leave the household life and study the Buddha’s teachings.
Subsequently, he realized the fruits of the path.
While traveling to teach in Northern India,
he encountered the extraordinary man Vāsumitra and explained to him that the Buddha had once prophesied he would succeed to the patriarchal position.
He immediately accepted him as his disciple.
When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to Vasumitra.
A verse says:
Where there is no mind, nothing can be apprehended; What is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.
If one realizes that the mind is not the mind, Only then does one fully understand the mind and its mental factors.
The Seventh Patriarch, Vasumitra:
A native of Northern India,
his clan name was Bharadvāja.
From the beginning, he constantly wore clean robes and held a single wine vessel,
his spirit and countenance remaining composed and natural.
No one could fathom him.
When he encountered Mīdhaka, [the latter] revealed their past karmic connection;
thereupon, [the king] cast aside his royal regalia and followed him to leave the household life.
Having realized the Way and received the full precepts,
he traveled to the kingdom of Kāmarūpa to convert Buddhadeva by means of debate.
Acting as his disciple,
when [the Master] was about to enter nirvana,
he entrusted the Dharma to him.
A verse was spoken:
The mind is identical to the realm of space; It demonstrates dharmas equal to space.
When the state of space is realized, There is neither "is" nor "is not."
The Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi,
was a native of the country of Kāmarūpa.
His clan name was Gautama.
He was born with a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown.
By nature he was exceedingly intelligent;
he could comprehend and memorize everything at a single reading.
When he had already reached the age of forty,
Vāsūmitra came to his native country,
whereupon he admired his preaching of the Dharma.
He followed him and left the household life;
having attained the Way and received the precepts,
he also devoted himself to traveling and transforming others through his teachings.
Upon arriving in the country of Tiqia,
he encountered the extraordinary person Vimalamitra and became his disciple.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to him and spoke this verse:
Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so.
If one realizes the nature of space, This is the penetration of the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā).
The Ninth Patriarch, Buddhabhadra. The Ninth Patriarch, Buddhabhadra.
He was a native of the country of Tiqia, of the Viśāla clan;
he had already reached the age of fifty at birth.
He had never spoken with his mouth,
nor had he ever set foot [upon such a path].
It happened that Buddhudana arrived at his house.
His parents intended to see him;
once they had seen Nandiya, he suddenly spoke of his own accord and walked forward toward them,
immediately expressing his wish for his teacher to renounce the household life.
Xun also attained the Way.
Having completed his observance of the precepts, he traveled to Central India for the purpose of conversion and there met the elder’s son, Gandhaka.
He was none other than the Venerable Pārśva.
Having taken him as his disciple,
he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
He then entrusted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"The True Principle is originally nameless; It is through names that the True Principle is revealed."
Having received the true Dharma, it is neither real nor false.
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Pārśva.
A native of Central India.
He remained in the womb for sixteen years before being born;
consequently, he was named Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Be Born).
He performed many miraculous deeds.
When the Buddha Nandimitra arrived in his kingdom,
his father, Gandhahastin, led him to the Buddha and requested that he be accepted as a disciple.
Furthermore, as a bhikṣu, he cultivated purity through ascetic practices;
day and night his ribs did not touch his mat,
and for this reason he was called the Venerable Pārśva.
While traveling and converting beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Puṣpa;
first he manifested auspicious signs,
and subsequently, he indeed obtained Pūrṇaśa.
He left the household life to become his disciple;
when [the Buddha] was about to pass into extinction,
he then entrusted the Dharma to him.
A verse was spoken:
The true essence is naturally true; Based on this truth, there is a principle to be understood.
Having realized the truly true Dharma, There is neither practice nor cessation.
The eleventh patriarch, Punyayasas, was a native of the country of Pataliputra.
His clan name was Gautama.
He possessed the nature of the Way from birth and knew in his own mind that he would encounter a holy teacher; thus,
when the Venerable Pārśva arrived in his kingdom, [he recognized him].
He then went to that dharma assembly;
as their discourse accorded with one another,
he immediately followed him and left the household life.
Having attained the Way, he traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to teach and transform others,
where he took Aśvaghoṣa as his disciple;
this was exactly in accordance with the Buddha’s prediction.
When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are not separate from one another.
Now I transmit the dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.
The Twelfth Patriarch, Aśvaghoṣa. The Twelfth Patriarch, Aśvaghoṣa.
A native of Vārāṇasī,
his family name is unknown;
he initially followed Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Having left the household life, he received the precepts.
His teacher explained his past affinity to him, saying:
"In the past, you once converted the people of a certain kingdom."
He was naked like a horse, yet he wailed piteously;
because he yearned for your virtue,
you were thus called "Horse-Wailing."
While traveling and converting others, he arrived at the kingdom of Puṣpagiri.
Thereupon, he subdued the great māra Kāpila-māra,
who was immediately brought under control and became his disciple.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma; light and darkness have always been non-dual.
Now I transmit this Dharma of realization, which is neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Kāṇhamata (迦毘摩羅). The Thirteenth Patriarch, Kāṇhamata.
He was a native of the state of Huashì;
his family name and given name are unknown.
Initially, he was a follower of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).
There was a master of great illusionist arts who went to visit Aśvaghoṣa;
when they compared their doctrines, he was not victorious.
He subsequently became a member of that school.
Having received the precepts of the Way,
he also traveled to propagate the teachings as far as Western India.
He subdued the great fire-dragon,
and by means of this, he obtained Nāgārjuna to become his disciple.
As he was about to pass into extinction, he entrusted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest; This is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
To realize this law of concealment and manifestation is neither folly nor wisdom.
(Verse 14) The Fourteenth Patriarch, Nāgārjuna.
He was a native of Western India.
His family name and clan are unknown.
He was profoundly intelligent and wise;
there was no worldly learning with which he was not thoroughly conversant.
In that country there is a mountain named Dragon-Victorious (Nāgavijaya).
On that mountain there formerly dwelt a divine dragon;
there was a great tree where he resided, capable of providing shade for the many dragons.
When Nāgārjuna attained a realization and desired to leave the household life,
he entered that mountain to rely upon a tree for his practice.
Having already been able to proclaim the Buddha-dharma for the multitude of dragons,
Kāpimāra learned his name and came to see him.
Nāgārjuna then paid homage to him as his teacher and received the precepts.
Traveling to propagate the Dharma,
he reached South India and met Kāṇadeva.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted his Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
"To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, I now explain the logic of liberation."
Not realizing the Dharma with the mind, neither anger nor joy—
Fifteenth Patriarch Kanadeva. The Fifteenth Patriarch, Kanadeva,
was a native of South India.
His surname was Viśāla.
When Nāgārjuna arrived at his house and gate,
he first sent a bowl filled with water to be placed before him.
Nādi then cast a single needle into the water;
he subsequently followed Nāgārjuna as his teacher, renounced the householder’s life,
and became one of his most eminent disciples.
Thereafter, he traveled to teach and transform beings until he reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu,
where he took Rāhula as his disciple;
when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to him.
A verse was spoken:
Originally, for the sake of those who transmit the Dharma, I explained the principle of liberation;
In reality, there is no realization within the Dharma, Neither end nor beginning.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, Rāhulata. The Sixteenth Patriarch Rāhulata was a native of Kapilavastu and belonged to the Brahman clan.
Having encountered Deva, he...
He obtained the karmic conditions for his family’s ear-whispering tree;
this was the teacher’s renunciation of the world,
through which he awakened to the Dharma and manifested extraordinary traces.
Thereafter, Saṃgharakṣita traveled through various regions to transform beings and arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
Following the Buddha’s prediction,
he sought out Saṃghanandi and soon found him, ordaining him as his disciple.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
In the reality of dharmas there is no realization; one neither grasps nor abandons them.
Since dharmas possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence, how could they arise internally or externally?
The Seventeenth Patriarch, Saṃghanandin. The Seventeenth Patriarch, Saṃghanandin.
He was a native of Śrāvastī,
of the Kṣatriya caste,
and the son of its king.
This refers to the Buddha Brahmadatta of old,
who manifested birth into a royal family and subsequently shaved his head and received the precepts within the royal palace.
He soon departed for a stone grotto on a famous mountain in that country to practice dhyāna.
There he encountered Rāhulabhadra at his place of meditation;
consequently, he submitted himself to him and sought further the essentials of the Dharma.
Rādhā then transmitted the Dharma to him.
Later, he went to the kingdom of Mathurā to seek out those who had inherited the Dharma as recorded by Rādhā.
He then obtained Gayāśata;
as he was entering parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
The mind-ground is fundamentally without birth; The ground of cultivation arises from conditions.
The seeds of conditions do not obstruct one another, And the flowers and fruits are likewise so.
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Gayasata. The Eighteenth Patriarch, Gayasata.
The people of the country of Māthura were of the Udraka clan;
throughout his life, he performed many miraculous feats.
When Saṃghanandin came to his house seeking him,
he followed his teacher to leave the household life and receive the precepts;
he immediately attained the transmission of the Dharma.
While traveling and converting others, he arrived at the kingdom of Yuezhi,
where he encountered Kumārajīva; for him,
he recounted the karmic conditions for his family’s extraordinary greatness and the origins of his auspicious dreams.
Kumāralata immediately followed him as his teacher and left the household life.
As [the teacher] was about to enter nirvana, he entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
There exists the seed and the ground of mind; through causes and conditions, the sprout is able to emerge.
When conditions do not obstruct one another, birth constantly gives rise to non-birth.

The Nineteenth Patriarch, Kumāralata. The Nineteenth Patriarch was Kumāralata. He said: "There exists the seed and the ground of mind; through causes and conditions, the sprout is able to emerge. When conditions do not obstruct one another, birth constantly gives rise to non-birth."
He was a native of the country of the Yuezhi,
of the Brahmin clan; from early on,
he was renowned as a man of unfathomable character.
Due to these conditions, he manifested birth here;
he soon found his teacher, Gayākāśyapa,
left the household life, and received the transmission of the Dharma.
He traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma and obtained Śāṇakavāsin as his disciple;
as he was about to pass away, he entrusted the Dharma to him.
A verse was spoken:
In the nature of things, there is fundamentally no arising; It is for the sake of those seeking [the truth] that the Dharma is taught.
Since nothing can be attained, why harbor doubts over what is or is not resolved?
The Twentieth Patriarch, Jayata.
Jayata was a native of Northern India;
his family name and clan are unknown.
When Kumāralata arrived in his native land,
he heard what [the Master] had said regarding karma spanning the three periods of time;
he was moved to realization and followed him.
Having left the household life and attained the Dharma,
he traveled through various kingdoms to transform beings until he reached the city of Rājagṛha,
where he took the bhikṣu Vāśpa as his disciple.
As he was about to pass into extinction, he entrusted [the Dharma] to him,
speaking this verse:
"Under these words, one accords with the unborn, Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm."

If one can understand in this way, having thoroughly mastered both phenomena and principle—this concludes [the section on] the twenty-first patriarch, Vāsukandra. The twenty-first patriarch was Vāsukandra.
He was a native of Rājagṛha,
of the Viśākha clan; while he was in the womb,
there were always holy monks present.
He informed his parents of his past karmic conditions;
upon his birth, great wonders occurred.
When he had grown slightly older, he followed the Arhat Prabhāsa to leave the household life.
He admired Kāśyapa and cultivated the dhūta practices;
subsequently, he met Śāṇavāsa and received the transmission of the Great Dharma.
He then traveled to the country of Nādikā to propagate the teachings.
Having obtained Māṇava as his disciple,
he was about to pass away and entrusted the Dharma to him,
speaking this verse:
Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded;
how could one fail to awaken and realize that the Dharma is contained therein? Neither of this age nor of antiquity.
The Twenty-second Patriarch, Mānara. The Twenty-second Patriarch, Mānara.
He was a native of the country of Nādi,
of the Kṣatriya caste, and the son of its king.
He possessed great supernatural powers.
His father, the King, commanded the master Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to ordain him;
having received the precepts, he was entrusted with the Dharma.
While traveling and teaching from Western India, he used his supernatural powers to transport himself to the kingdom of Yuezhi.
There, he found the bhikṣu Helena,
to whom he immediately entrusted the Dharma.
He soon entered parinirvāṇa.
His verse of entrusting the Dharma says:
"The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, the reality is profoundly deep."
Recognizing the nature within the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
The Twenty-third Patriarch, Hòulènná (Haklenā).
He was a native of the country of Yuezhi.
He was of the Brahmin caste.
From the time he was in the womb until his birth,
there were many extraordinary signs.
He subsequently followed a bhikṣu who was an arhat to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
He constantly dwelt in the forest reciting the sūtras;
due to his karmic conditions from former lives, a flock of cranes came to rely upon him.
Thus he received his title.
Later, through Manoratha, he attained the Dharma and traveled to teach and transform beings as far as the kingdom of Central India.
He obtained the bhikṣu Siṃha as his disciple and, intending to pass away, entrusted the Dharma to him.
He further instructed him, saying: "Go to another country."
If there is peril in that land,
it will fall upon your person; therefore,
be careful to entrust [the teaching] to others early.
Do not allow it to be severed.
The verse says:
When one recognizes the nature of mind, it may be called inconceivable.
Thoroughly realized, there is nothing to be attained; when attained, one does not speak of knowing.
This was the twenty-fourth patriarch, the Bhikṣu Siṃha. The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Bhikṣu Siṃha.
He was a native of Central India,
of the Brahmin caste.
Having left home in his youth, he practiced meditative concentration.
Later, he again studied under Śīlabhadra,
receiving the transmission of the Great Dharma.
He then went to convert the people in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
First, there were many who converted those of other schools, such as Dharmadatta and others; later,
he obtained the son of an elder, Sthavira,
and resolved his karmic connection regarding the grasping of the pearl.
He then accepted him and ordained him as a monk.
Because of their past affinity, he bestowed upon him the name Vasiṣṭha.
Once Vasiṣṭha had received the precepts, Siṃha said to him:
Having just observed this country,
they will surely impose hardships upon me;
how could I seek a mere escape?
"The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata, which I have transmitted, I now entrust to you.
You should uphold it,
and immediately depart to devote yourself to its propagation and transformation."
Should there be anyone who harbors doubts,
I shall take my saṃghāṭī robe as a token of faith and speak this verse:
When speaking of knowing and seeing, knowing and seeing are both the mind;
when the mind is present, that is knowing and seeing—knowing and seeing are right here and now.
The Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha. The Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha.
He was a native of Kaśmīra.
His family name was Brahmin. Because the local dialects differed from those of his original biography, his name appears three times; he possessed extraordinary signs at birth.
Having encountered the Lion,
he discussed their past karmic affinity with him and subsequently became his disciple.
Knowing that he himself was in danger,
the Master pre-emptively entrusted the Dharma to him;
Sthavira then departed.
Having traveled through Central India and South India,
he performed many extraordinary conversions;
consequently, he gained the son of the King of South India, Ajātaśatru, as a follower.
He shall become his disciple and accompany him back to the realm he previously transformed;
when [the Buddha] is about to pass into extinction, he will entrust the Dharma to him.
A verse was spoken:
The Sages speak of knowledge and vision; Within the objective realm, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
I have now awakened to true nature: There is no path, nor is there any principle.
The twenty-sixth patriarch was Ramaputta (不如蜜多).
